title: Review: Transcription; Translation; How enzymes work
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: GE05a#t3 term and clue written for the game; GE05a#t4 term and clue written for the game; EZ01b#t3 term and clue written for the game; GE04a#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EZ01a#N.10a, EZ01b#N.9, GE04a#N.11, GE05a#N.10, EZ01a#N.11, EZ01b#N.6, GE04a#N.3a, GE05a#N.4, EZ01a#N.2a, EZ01b#N.8b, GE04a#N.5, GE05a#N.7. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Anticodon
items.clue: Three bases on one loop of a clover-leaf molecule, complementary to a triplet on mRNA.

items.label: Peptide bond
items.clue: Link formed by a condensation reaction between the amino acids on two tRNAs at the ribosome.

items.label: Enzyme–substrate complex
items.clue: Formed when a reactant molecule collides with the active site the right way round, then binds.

items.label: RNA polymerase
items.clue: Enzyme that binds at the start of a gene and joins adjacent nucleotides of the new transcript.

questions.stem: Lipase catalyses the hydrolysis of triglycerides but has no effect on starch. What is the reason?

options.text: Starch molecules are too large to enter the active site, but any molecule smaller than starch could.
The active site of lipase is complementary in shape and chemical properties to a triglyceride only.
Starch requires more energy to break down than lipase is able to supply to the reaction.
Lipase seeks out triglyceride molecules in the fluid and ignores starch molecules it meets.

questions.explanation: Specificity arises from the structure of the active site: its shape and chemical properties match one substrate, so starch cannot bind in a way that allows catalysis.

questions.stem: Hexokinase is the enzyme that adds a phosphate group to glucose. X-ray structures show that the two halves of the enzyme are further apart when no glucose is bound. When glucose binds, the two halves close around it. What does this evidence show?

options.text: It supports the lock-and-key model, as glucose fits an active site of fixed shape.
It shows that glucose denatures hexokinase, because the shape of the enzyme changes.
It shows the lock-and-key model was worthless, as it explained nothing about enzymes.
It supports the induced-fit model: the active site changes shape as substrate binds.

questions.stem: α-Amanitin, a toxin from the death cap mushroom, blocks the RNA polymerase that makes mRNA in eukaryotic cells. It has no effect on DNA polymerase or on ribosomes. Which prediction about liver cells exposed to it is correct?

options.text: DNA replication stops, because the cells can no longer separate their DNA strands.
Translation of mRNA already in the cytoplasm stops at once.
No new mRNA is made, so protein synthesis falls as the existing mRNA is broken down.
The DNA of the cells' genes is damaged, so their base sequences change.

questions.explanation: Without RNA polymerase there is no transcription and no new mRNA. Proteins are made only until the existing mRNA runs out.

questions.stem: The coding region of an mRNA, from the first nucleotide of the start codon to the last nucleotide of the stop codon, is 903 nucleotides long. How many amino acids does the polypeptide translated from this region contain?
questions.explanation: 903 ÷ 3 = 301 codons. AUG codes for methionine and the stop codon codes for nothing, so the polypeptide has 301 − 1 = 300 amino acids.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical bacterium, enzyme E catalyses the conversion of compound A to compound B. The conversion of A to B releases energy. A mutation stops the bacterium from making enzyme E. No other enzyme in the bacterium acts on compound A. Which prediction about compound B in the mutant bacterium is best supported?

options.text: B no longer forms at all, as A cannot change into B without enzyme E.
B forms at the normal rate, as the bacterium makes a new enzyme because it needs B.
B forms at the normal rate, as ATP supplies the energy that enzyme E used to supply.
B still forms, but far more slowly, as the reaction is no longer catalysed.

questions.stem: According to the induced-fit model, what happens when a substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme?

options.text: Both the enzyme and the substrate change shape as they bind.
The rigid active site admits only an exactly matching substrate.
The active site closes around a substrate that keeps its shape.
The enzyme seizes the substrate and holds it without any changes.

questions.explanation: Both change shape when binding occurs. The closer fit strains bonds within the substrate, which is part of how catalysis is achieved.

questions.stem: A section of the DNA template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGCAT. What is the base sequence of the RNA transcribed from this section?

options.text: UACGCAU
AUGCGUA
UAGCGAU
ATGCGTA

questions.explanation: Each RNA base is complementary to the template base: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, giving AUGCGUA.

questions.stem: A cell contains many different kinds of tRNA molecule. What is the role of a tRNA during translation?

options.text: It binds to a codon first and then collects from the cytoplasm whichever amino acid that codon specifies.
It brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome and pairs its anticodon with the matching codon on the mRNA.
It delivers an amino acid and remains bonded to it, becoming part of the finished polypeptide chain.
It carries the mRNA bases that the ribosome converts into the amino acids of the polypeptide.

questions.explanation: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid, so base pairing at the ribosome delivers the amino acid the codon specifies.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how an enzyme acts as a catalyst in a cell?

options.text: It is converted into product along with the substrate, so the cell must keep making it.
It makes possible a reaction that could not take place at all in its absence in the cell.
It transfers energy to the substrate so that the reaction is driven forward faster.
It increases the rate of a reaction that could occur without it, and is released unchanged.

questions.explanation: Enzymes are catalysts: they increase the rate of reactions that would otherwise occur far too slowly at cell temperature, and each molecule catalyses the reaction repeatedly.

questions.stem: Trypsin is made by cells in the pancreas and digests proteins in the small intestine. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Trypsin is extracellular because it is made outside cells, in the pancreatic juice.
Trypsin is intracellular because proteins are digested inside the cells lining the small intestine.
Trypsin is extracellular: it is made inside pancreatic cells, secreted, and acts in the small intestine.
Trypsin is intracellular because it is made inside cells, like every enzyme.

questions.explanation: Made inside cells, secreted by exocytosis, acting outside cells: that is an extracellular enzyme.

questions.stem: During transcription, what holds each RNA nucleotide in position against the DNA template strand while it is being added to the growing RNA?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, which break again when the RNA is released.
Covalent bonds made by RNA polymerase between the RNA base and the DNA base opposite it.
Hydrogen bonds between identical bases, so the RNA is an exact copy of the template.
Hydrogen bonds between adenine and thymine, since RNA contains the same four bases as DNA.

questions.stem: An antibiotic stops the ribosome from moving along the mRNA but does not affect the binding of tRNAs or the formation of peptide bonds. What effect will this have on translation of an mRNA?

options.text: Only the first peptide bond forms, since the next codon cannot be moved into place for a tRNA to bind.
Translation is unaffected, because all the tRNAs bind along the mRNA before any peptide bonds are formed.
Translation is unaffected, because each tRNA leaves the ribosome before the next one binds to the mRNA.
The chain still grows, because each tRNA stays attached to its amino acid and the next tRNA simply joins onto it.
